items.passage: We kept a tailoring shop in Tehran on a street with too many tailors, and by the third winter our ledger ran mostly red. My brother Kemoy cut the cloth; I, Hemi, did the seams and the slow finishing. Every coat that left the shop carried a small linen tag in its collar, stitched with a single letter: K. When a colonel's wife admired a coat in the window, Kemoy thanked her at the counter while I sat in the back with pins in my mouth. That evening on the roof, where we hung the shop's linen to dry, I said a good deal. For a month afterward we pegged our cloths at opposite ends of the line. One coat came back for mending in February with its tag cut out, and neither of us asked who had done it. In March I went up to take in the new tags Kemoy had washed and starched. Each one read K. and H., the second letter in his clumsier hand. He came up behind me with the basket and pegged his shirts beside mine.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A customer's praise exposes how unevenly two brothers share the work on each coat.
A set of new tags shows the brothers preparing to change how their shop is run.
A dispute over the shop's failing ledger is what drives the brothers' quarrel on the roof.
An old grievance about credit is answered by a gesture made in place of an apology.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 모든 코트의 꼬리표에 K만 새겨지고 손님의 칭찬도 Kemoy가 받자, 화자는 지붕에서 말다툼을 하고 두 사람은 빨랫줄 양 끝으로 갈라선다. 뒷부분에서 Kemoy는 말없이 K와 H가 함께 적힌 새 꼬리표를 손수 만들어 널고 화자 옆에 빨래를 건다. 두 사건을 연결하면 공로를 둘러싼 서운함이 사과의 말이 아니라 행동으로 응답받았다는 것이 요지이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 첫 사건만, B는 둘째 사건의 표면만 말하며, C는 지문에 근거 없는 장부 문제를 다툼의 원인으로 삼는다.

items.passage: Dry leaves choked the stone basin of the fountain in our courtyard in Taipei, and every October Baoyu came to argue with me about them. He had been my father's closest friend; he arrived with a rake and insisted the leaves be burned, and I insisted they be left to rot into the flower beds. My father had sailed for Fujian when I was nine. Baoyu asked after my schooling, my cough, the price of rice, and never once after him. We argued for six autumns, loudly enough that the neighbors leaned from their windows to listen. One year he set a small tin box on the fountain's rim while we shouted, and carried it home again when he left. The seventh October he did not come. A boy brought the rake and the tin box to our gate. Inside was a photograph of a young man in shirtsleeves raking leaves into that same basin, and on its back, in my father's hand, the year I was born. I leaned the rake against the fountain and left the leaves where they lay.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A minor yearly dispute turns out to have carried a larger matter left unnamed.
An old family friend keeps up an autumn chore after the narrator's father leaves.
A box left at the gate gives the narrator a record of her father's own habits.
The narrator's refusal to burn the leaves is what leads Baoyu to stop visiting.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 여섯 해 동안 이어진 낙엽 다툼은 사소해 보이지만, Baoyu는 모든 것을 묻으면서도 화자의 아버지 이야기만은 꺼내지 않는다. 중간의 상자는 열리지 않은 채 남고, 뒷부분에서 그 상자 속 사진이 아버지가 같은 분수대에서 낙엽을 긁던 모습임이 드러난다. 두 사건을 함께 읽으면 낙엽 다툼이 말하지 못한 아버지의 부재를 대신해 온 것이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 첫 사건만, C는 둘째 사건의 표면만 말하고, D는 지문이 제시하지 않은 인과를 세운다.

items.passage: Brine and coal smoke: that was the smell of the crossing on the salt flats east of Manchester, where my father ran the little ferry over the brine channel for thirty years. Each spring a passenger named Josiah bought two tickets and rode alone at the stern, hat in his hands, and left the second ticket tucked into the rail. My father punched both and never asked. The winter after my father died, the engine began to cough, and the yard at Irlam offered me three possible weeks in April for the overhaul. I took the second. Josiah's Tuesday fell in it; my father had chalked that date on the wheelhouse wall every year, and I had not washed it off. "Repairs," I said, when Josiah came down the path that morning. "Engine won't be ready till the summer trade." I untied my father's old skiff from the jetty, set the oars in their locks, and held the bow steady while he stepped in. On the far bank I took a ticket punch from my coat.
items.question: Based on the text, why does the narrator most likely choose the second week in April for the repairs?
options: She needs the engine mended before the busier summer trade on the channel.
She wants to spare Josiah a crossing on the boat her father used to run.
She hopes a delay will lead Josiah to explain the second ticket at last.
She wants to carry Josiah across in person on the day he always comes.
items.explanation: 화자가 직접 내세운 이유는 여름 장사 전에 엔진을 고친다는 것이지만, 세 주 가운데 굳이 Josiah가 오는 화요일이 든 주를 골랐다는 점은 이것만으로 설명되지 않는다. 앞부분에서 아버지가 매년 그날을 조타실 벽에 적어 두고 두 장의 표를 말없이 찍어 주던 습관이 제시된다. 끝에서 화자는 아버지의 작은 배로 직접 노를 저어 그를 건네고 표 펀치를 꺼낸다. 따라서 그날 몸소 그를 건네 주려는 D가 정답이며, A는 표면 명분, B와 C는 날짜 선택과 직접 노를 젓는 행동을 함께 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: When I was sixteen, my violin lessons took place in the back room of a seed-saving cooperative in Tromso, between shelves of labeled envelopes: dwarf peas, northern kale, a barley nobody had sown since 1950. Anders sorted seeds while I played and corrected my bowing without looking up: "Again, Aydin." In March he mentioned, between two envelopes, that he had entered me in the conservatory audition in Oslo, with a sonata of his choosing. I said thank you in the voice one saves for parking fines. For three months I practiced the sonata, and he sorted, and neither of us brought up the form. Once I caught him holding an envelope, not sorting it, while I took the slow movement twice. The night before the train, I found that envelope in my violin case: barley, 1950, keep dry. I now live in a city with no frost to speak of. I keep it in the drawer where the rosin goes, and I check the seal each winter.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Wry and detached toward a teacher whose choice the narrator recalls
Wry and relieved toward a decision that spared the narrator a choice
Wry and grateful toward a teacher who acted on the narrator's behalf
Wry and grateful toward the years the narrator spent in Tromso
items.explanation: 앞부분은 '주차 위반 딱지에 쓰는 목소리' 같은 표현과 건조한 나열로 묻지도 않고 결정한 선생님에 대한 냉소적 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 선생님이 봉투를 분류하지 않고 든 채 화자의 연주를 듣는 장면이 어긋나는 디테일로 놓인다. 끝에서 화자는 그 봉투를 지금도 송진 서랍에 두고 겨울마다 봉인을 확인하는데, 이는 선생님에 대한 고마움을 감정어 없이 보여 준다. 따라서 C가 정답이며, A는 겉 층만, B는 속 층의 원인을 안도로 뒤집었고, D는 대상을 트롬쇠 시절 전체로 넓혔다.

items.passage: When the last crate of my father's records was sold, Ofelia counted the bills twice on the folding table between the lemon sellers and the fish stalls of the Valparaiso market. I had called her Señora all morning, as I called the woman who ran the bakery, and she answered to it. The plan had been hers: sell the records before the rent came due and keep me at the same school. A man in a striped scarf carried off the jazz albums; a student took the rest in two trips. Ofelia divided the bills into two stacks, slid the thicker one toward me, and said, "For the rent, Emiliano. Count it." The thinner one went into her apron. At the empanada cart she bought one, handed it to me, and said she had already eaten. On the walk uphill she carried the empty crates. That night the rent envelope on the kitchen table was thicker than the stack I had counted, and her apron hung on its hook, the pocket flat.
items.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Ofelia and Emiliano?
options: Emiliano keeps Ofelia at a formal distance, while she quietly bears costs on his behalf.
Emiliano treats Ofelia as a respected elder, while she accepts the formal role he gives.
Emiliano and Ofelia work as partners in a sale, while they split what their plan earns.
Emiliano helps Ofelia through a hard morning, while she relies on him to finish the sale.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Emiliano는 Ofelia를 빵집 주인과 똑같이 'Señora'라고 부르며 거리를 둔다. 중간에서 돈은 두꺼운 묶음이 Emiliano 쪽으로 가고, Ofelia는 자기 것은 사지 않고 그에게만 엠파나다를 사 준다. 끝에서 집세 봉투가 그가 센 돈보다 두꺼워지고 그녀의 앞치마 주머니는 비어 있어, 그녀가 자기 몫까지 조용히 내놓았음이 드러난다. 따라서 A가 정답이며, B는 호칭만, C는 시장 장면만 반영하고, D는 돌봄의 방향을 뒤집었다.

items.passage: Four rules held in the tailor's back room, which Weiqi and I rented on alternate mornings that Vermont winter to proof our dough: no talk of prices, no borrowed flour, no opening the window, and nothing of mine crosses the chalk line on the floor. I had drawn that line myself, heel to heel across the boards, and each Monday I knelt and traced it fresh. Weiqi, whose bakery stood three doors from mine, kept to her side without comment. On a Thursday in February a letter came addressed to the tailor, and Weiqi opened it, thinking it was hers. The building would be sold in spring. She read it aloud to me anyway, from her side, and then we stood a long while among the rising bowls. The following Monday I knelt with the chalk in my hand, as always. My name is Matheus. I set the chalk back in its tin, and when Weiqi's bowl of rye needed the warmer corner, I lifted it across myself.
items.question: Based on the text, what does the chalk line most likely represent?
options: A practical rule that lets two tenants share a single rented room
Matheus's wish to guard his methods from a competing baker
A lost friendship between the bakers that the letter restores
A separation Matheus had insisted on, which he no longer keeps
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 분필 선은 Matheus가 직접 긋고 매주 월요일 다시 그리는 규칙의 일부로, 경쟁자와의 거리를 유지하는 장치로 등장한다. 중간에 건물이 팔린다는 편지를 함께 듣고 두 사람이 한참 서 있는 장면이 선을 대하는 방식의 전환점이 된다. 끝에서 그는 분필을 다시 상자에 넣고 Weiqi의 반죽 그릇을 직접 선 너머로 옮긴다. 따라서 그가 고집해 온 거리와 그것을 더는 지키지 않음을 함께 담은 D가 정답이며, A는 문자적 기능, B는 앞 맥락만, C는 지문에 없는 과거의 우정을 가정한다.

items.passage: When the power failed across Old Dhaka, the night pharmacy where Tara worked became the only lit room on the lane, and by midnight two families had carried their festival trays to its single steel counter. Tara's aunt laid out rice pudding for Eid. Hari, who had sailed cargo ships for thirty years and now rented the room above the shop, came down with a brass plate of marigolds and sweets for his evening prayer. Three times he set it near the corner; three times, when an arm reached past him, he drew it back against his chest. Hari's plate stayed at the counter's rim, a skiff riding out the night beyond the harbor lights. Tara moved two bowls and left a space. He looked at it and held the plate level. Later her aunt spooned pudding onto a leaf, set it on the empty steel, and pushed it a finger's width toward him. The marigolds went into the middle, and his small lamp leaned toward the rice.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase "a skiff riding out the night beyond the harbor lights" most nearly suggests that Hari
options: is weighed down by the plate he has carried for his evening prayer.
has fixed the counter's rim as a boundary he intends to keep.
is waiting outside the gathering until a place is offered to him.
is falling back on habits formed during his years on cargo ships.
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 정전으로 두 가족이 하나뿐인 계산대에 몰려든 상황과, Hari가 접시를 세 번 내려놓았다가 다시 끌어당기는 반복 행동이 제시된다. 비유 뒤에서 Tara가 만든 빈자리에는 움직이지 않다가, 이모가 그를 향해 음식을 밀어 준 뒤에야 접시를 가운데로 옮긴다. 따라서 이 비유는 Hari가 모임 바깥에 머물며 맞아들여지기를 기다리고 있음을 뜻하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 무게, B는 경계라는 다른 속성만 읽었고, D는 선원 경력이라는 문자적 연상에 머문다.

items.passage: Years later I can still see Angus at the crossing below Kelvin Mill, where the burn had dried that August to a bed of grey stones. I clerked for him three mornings a week, long after he had left the bench; he called me Miss Maeve and nothing shorter. In his breast pocket he kept an envelope addressed, in his own hand, to a man he had once sentenced, and its corners had gone soft as cloth. Each morning at the near edge of the stones he pressed two fingers flat against that pocket, stood a while, and turned us toward the bridge. For him the letter was a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer. I would wait with the satchel. On the last dry morning he went out as far as the middle, sat on a flat rock long enough to read a page, and came back with the pocket buttoned. We went round by the bridge, as before.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase "a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer" most nearly suggests that the letter is
options: a weight that presses on Angus each time he sets out in the morning.
a barrier that conditions outside Angus keep placing in his way.
a duty left from his years on the bench that still orders his days.
an effort Angus resumes each day without bringing it to an end.
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 Angus는 예전에 판결한 사람에게 쓴 편지를 모서리가 닳도록 지니고 다니며, 매일 아침 돌밭 가장자리에서 주머니를 누르고는 다리 쪽으로 돌아서는 행동을 반복한다. 비유 뒤에서 그는 마지막 날 강바닥 한가운데까지 나가지만 주머니 단추를 채운 채 돌아오고 여전히 다리로 돌아간다. 따라서 이 비유는 매일 다시 시도하지만 끝내 마치지 못하는 노력을 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 무게, B는 외부 장애라는 다른 속성을 읽었고, C는 판사 경력으로 의미를 넓혔다.

items.passage:
Smell of split guava, sweet and gone to vinegar,
the wasps loud in it. In March the deed changed hands;
Ximena paid the last wage in an envelope
and wrote the new gate code on its flap.
Still, each dawn, Kiara walks the rows above Kingston
lifting what the wind brought down,
binding cracked limbs to their stakes with green twine,
the same knot, the same three turns, tree after tree.
She moves among them, a candle trimmed for a ship already moored,
and the light comes up behind her over the Blue Mountains.
Ximena watches from the porch, her coffee going cold,
and says nothing of the clearing crew due in June.
At dusk Kiara rinses the twine knife at the cistern,
wipes it on her skirt, and hangs her ring of keys
on the gatepost nail where anyone could take them,
then walks down the hill toward the road.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase "a candle trimmed for a ship already moored" most nearly suggests that Kiara's work is
options: a devotion she keeps up though no one now requires it of her.
a strength that is wearing away the longer she stays on.
a bid to be noticed and kept on by the orchard's new owner.
the plain habit of a worker used to rising before daylight.
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 과수원은 이미 팔리고 마지막 임금까지 지급된 상황이며, Kiara는 그래도 매일 새벽 같은 매듭으로 나뭇가지를 묶는 일을 반복한다. 비유 뒤에서 그녀는 열쇠를 누구나 가져갈 수 있는 문기둥에 걸어 두고 길로 내려가므로, 일자리를 지키려는 행동이 아님이 드러난다. 따라서 이 비유는 더 이상 아무도 요구하지 않는데도 이어 가는 헌신을 뜻하므로 A가 정답이다. B는 소진, C는 고용 유지라는 다른 해석이며, D는 새벽에 일어나는 습관이라는 문자적 해석이다.

items.passage: Rosedale, Mississippi, still keeps its salt-water pool, fed by a brackish well the town drilled in 1958 and never managed to sweeten. Aaliyah came back to survey the levee and found Darnell, the keeper, raking leaves off the surface as he had when she was ten. The water sat an inch lower on the tiles each year, he said, and each Sunday he ran the pump an hour to bring it back. She had left on a scholarship at seventeen, one of four the county gave that spring; on the honor board by the bathhouse, the other three names had addresses in Memphis and Chicago pencilled under them. In her notes that night she called the scholarship a sluice gate the town had opened for its own children. The next morning she measured the pool wall with her rod and logged the figure. Before she drove off, she ran the pump for an hour herself, though it was Tuesday.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase "a sluice gate the town had opened for its own children" most nearly suggests that the scholarship was
options: a route to wider success that the town proudly offered to its youth.
an opening the town made itself that slowly let its young flow away.
a barrier that let the town decide which of its children could go.
a structure meant to manage the water that the levee holds back.
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 수영장 물이 해마다 조금씩 줄어드는 상황과, Darnell이 매주 펌프로 물을 다시 채우는 반복 행동이 제시된다. 또 장학금을 받은 다른 세 명의 이름 아래에는 멤피스와 시카고 주소가 적혀 있어 젊은이들이 돌아오지 않았음을 암시한다. 비유 뒤에서 Aaliyah가 평일인데도 직접 펌프를 돌리는 장면은 빠져나간 것을 되채우려는 몸짓으로 읽힌다. 따라서 마을이 스스로 열어 젊은이들을 조금씩 내보낸 통로라는 B가 정답이며, A는 성공의 통로, C는 선별 장벽이라는 다른 속성만 읽었고, D는 문자적 해석이다.

items.passage: By the ninth night before the Lantern Festival, Yuying and I had swept the barbershop on Drum Tower Lane so often that its floor shone. Our master had promised the guild that she would sing the opening verse on its stage, and she had never sung for anyone but me, Meilin, who shared the night shift with her. Each night, once the shutters were barred, she sang it through twice, low and exact; whenever boots sounded in the lane, she stopped mid-line and took up the broom again. Her voice was a razor stropped every evening and laid back in its case. I held the lamp and kept time with my foot on the board. Two nights later a drunk porter knocked to ask the hour, and she finished the verse before she unbarred the shutter to answer him.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase "a razor stropped every evening and laid back in its case" most nearly suggests that Yuying's voice is
options: a sharp edge that could wound whoever happened to overhear it.
a gift that is still too rough to be offered on a public stage.
a readiness she sharpens each night and keeps from public trial.
one of the tools of the trade she practices in the barbershop.
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 Yuying은 길드 무대에서 노래하기로 되어 있지만 화자 외에는 누구 앞에서도 불러 본 적이 없다는 상황이 제시된다. 또 매일 밤 정확하게 두 번 연습하면서도 골목에 발소리가 나면 노래를 멈추는 행동을 반복한다. 비유 뒤에서 그녀는 문을 두드리는 사람이 있어도 끝까지 노래를 마치는데, 이는 목소리가 이미 준비되어 있음을 보여 준다. 따라서 매일 갈고닦았지만 남 앞에서는 시험하지 않는 준비를 뜻하는 C가 정답이며, A는 날카로움, B는 미숙함이라는 다른 속성을 읽었고, D는 이발 도구라는 문자적 해석이다.

items.passage: Eulalio set the copper pot on the boarding-house stove each evening and made you repeat the farewells until the beans went soft. In the valley, he told you, a guest does not simply leave; the leaving has an order, and he drilled you in it, correcting the place of each word, the pause before the blessing, the second thanks for the salt. For six weeks, Anacleto, you practiced while the landlady shelled peas by the window. Then your coach for Puebla was moved up a day. That morning you stood at the kitchen door with your bag, ready to recite the whole of it. His own farewell was ______. He touched two fingers to your sleeve, said a single word, and turned back to stir the pot before you could begin.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: deliberately brief
hastily curt
properly ceremonial
carefully rehearsed
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Eulalio는 작별의 순서와 말 한마디의 위치까지 고쳐 주며 인사를 매우 신중하게 다루는 인물로 그려진다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그는 소매에 손가락 두 개를 대고 한 단어만 말한 뒤 돌아서는데, 이는 짧지만 의도된 동작이다. 따라서 의도성과 짧음을 함께 만족하는 A가 정답이다. B는 짧음만 맞고 앞의 신중함과 어긋나며, C는 앞의 의례만 반영해 뒤의 한 단어와 맞지 않고, D는 연습이라는 지문의 주제어를 빌렸을 뿐 그가 연습한 쪽이 아니라는 점과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Aluva station, at the far end of the Kochi metro line, was empty at six except for you, Priya, and Vikram with a cardboard box. For eleven years of rehearsals he had wound the brass metronome himself before every session, and if a cellist reached for it, he moved it a few inches away without breaking his sentence. His mother's house in Kakkanad had been emptied that week; the piano was sold, the shelves taken apart, and the box held the last thing left. He took out the metronome and handed it to you, the youngest of the second violins, in a manner that was ______. Then he folded the empty box flat, did not stay to watch you try the key, and stepped onto the train before the doors finished chiming.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: fondly sentimental
briskly dismissive
quietly trusting
steadily rhythmic
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Vikram은 11년 동안 메트로놈을 아무에게도 맡기지 않고 직접 태엽을 감아 왔으므로, 그것을 건네는 일 자체가 신뢰를 뜻한다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그는 상자를 접고 화자가 태엽을 감아 보는 것을 지켜보지도 않은 채 떠나는데, 이는 감정을 드러내지 않고 맡기는 태도다. 따라서 두 단서를 함께 만족하는 C가 정답이다. A는 감정의 정도가 지나치고, B는 뒤의 동작만 반영해 앞의 소중함과 어긋나며, D는 메트로놈이라는 소재에서 빌린 표현이다.
